#4643. Unit1 FARO and NEON review: I just found my new favorite e-bike helmets

I test a lot of electric bikes, which means I also spend a lot of time wearing bicycle helmets. And while most helmets tend to fall into the decidedly unexciting category of “necessary safety equipment,” UNIT 1 has managed to make a couple that I actually get excited about wearing.

I’ve been using both the UNIT 1 FARO and the new NEON, and despite taking fairly different approaches, they’ve both become regular go-to helmets for me.

The FARO is the more futuristic-looking of the two, and it’s also the one that really leans into the “smart helmet” concept.

The helmet includes MIPS protection to reduce rotational impact during a collision, as well as integrated lighting on both the front and rear, including a large customizable rear lighting area made up of dozens of LEDs.

That large rear LED array is a feature I particularly appreciate since visibility is such a major part of cycling safety.

A helmet obviously can’t force drivers to pay attention, but I’d rather give them as many opportunities as possible to see me. The hidden light area below the obvious LED light bar adds a lot of extra visibility.

You can see just how vivid it is in the GIF below, though in real life it looks even better!

The FARO’s lighting system works with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote, which adds turn signals controlled right from the bars.

The system can also provide automatic brake-light functionality, giving you another way to communicate with traffic around you.

I’ll admit that turn signals on bicycles can sometimes feel a bit gimmicky, especially when they’re so close together that drivers can’t really tell which direction is flashing. But putting them high up on the helmet makes them considerably more visible, and the little wireless handlebar remote makes operating them incredibly easy.

The rechargeable lighting is also convenient. I’ve topped up the helmet from a power bank while out and about, meaning you don’t necessarily need to find a wall outlet if you realize your helmet is running low. The rear LED light bar also turns green and illuminates along the length of the bar to let you know what percentage of charge the battery has reached. The only way it could be clearer would be with a screen, but we’re still talking about a helmet here, not a phone.

There are other smart features packed in too, including crash detection and app-based customization.

The tradeoff is weight. At around 640 grams for a medium, the FARO is noticeably heavier than a conventional bicycle helmet. It doesn’t bother me much once I’m riding, and I’ve found the helmet comfortable, but you definitely know there’s more helmet up there. Each time I pick it up, I’m reminded that it’s not just the basic little foam shell that I’ve been wearing for the last few years.

Then there’s the price. At around $230 (or $195 during the current Black Friday sale period), this isn’t a cheap helmet. You’re paying for all of that technology, lighting, and design.

As much as I like the FARO, I’ve also become a big fan of the UNIT 1 NEON.

At roughly 430 grams in a medium, it’s significantly lighter than the FARO, and that difference is immediately noticeable. It’s also a bit cheaper at around $210 (or $178 during the Black Friday sale period) while still packing several of the smart features that make UNIT 1’s helmets interesting.

You still get MIPS rotational protection, crash detection, integrated rear lighting, app connectivity, and compatibility with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote for turn signals and brake-light functionality.

I do wish the NEON had a front light like the FARO. That’s probably the biggest feature I miss when switching between the two. But the NEON makes up for it with one of my favorite features on either helmet: its magnetic face shield.

The shield is ridiculously easy to attach and remove. You don’t even need to carefully line it up. I just need to get it somewhere near the mounting points with one hand and the powerful magnets basically grab it out of the air and snap it into position.

That means I can easily add or remove it one-handed, even while riding.

The photochromic shield is clear enough for night riding but darkens when exposed to bright sunlight, giving you sun protection without requiring separate daytime and nighttime shields. I’ve found that incredibly convenient, especially on rides that transition from daylight into evening. I hate that I can’t wear my sunglasses for eye protection at night, and a lens like this solves that issue.

The NEON also gets something particularly important for faster e-bike riders: NTA 8776 certification. That’s the Dutch standard designed specifically around higher-speed e-bike uses at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). For the Class 3 e-bikes that have become increasingly common in the US, that’s a big distinction compared to helmets rated for crashes at slower speeds.

That’s actually difficult, because I regularly use both.

The FARO is the one I’d choose if maximum visibility and technology were my priorities. I love having LEDs both front and rear, the MIPS protection, and the handlebar-controlled turn signals. It’s comfortable, looks great, and has become one of my favorite urban riding helmets.

But the NEON may be the easier helmet to recommend to most e-bike riders.

It’s lighter, a little cheaper, still gives you a rear light and smart safety features, has that excellent magnetic photochromic face shield, and importantly carries NTA 8776 certification for faster e-bike riding.

Neither helmet is inexpensive, and the FARO in particular asks you to accept some extra weight in exchange for all that technology. But I’m used to wearing much heavier motorcycle helmets and ways.

Plus, it’s important to note that these aren’t helmets I tested for a few rides and then tossed onto a shelf. Both have stayed in my regular rotation, and I find myself reaching for them frequently when I head out on an e-bike. The fact that I not only enjoyed them during my testing but actually replaced my old helmets with them should speak for itself.

For someone who rides as much as I do, that’s probably the strongest endorsement I can give them.

Between solid helmets like these and safe riding clothing, it’s good to feel protected!

#4642. Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

Published Nov 11, 2026 12:01 PM EST

The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” said Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

In the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband company Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

Although the new strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

“The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” said Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”

#4641. RJ Mitte's Death Highlights Mental Health Challenges for People With Cerebral Palsy

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have said the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

Mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

There is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:

If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research shows that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou said.

“However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

“While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

“If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

“Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou said.

“Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”

#4640. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

#4639. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#4638. Chunky mama bear wins 2026 Nope award for quick retreat from bigger rival

Published Nov 11, 2026 1:12 PM EST

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she said, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4636. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

#4634. Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

Published Nov 11, 2026 2:00 PM EST

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

“Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”

#4632. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4631. Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

Teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

The launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The company was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a new generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

The Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Even so, important features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

And with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

The Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced says preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

At $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

#4630. Stock up on Blu-rays and box sets during the annual Barnes & Noble 50% off Criterion Collection sale

If you’ve been saving money for Black Friday, there has been a change of plans. Every year, Barnes & Noble slashes prices on Criterion collection movies and box sets by half. It’s the next best thing to being in the Criterion Closet. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs in the Criterion sale are $24.99, the bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and the big director box sets are half off too. B&N ships orders of $60 or more for free, so three of the $24.99 4K discs clear the bar. The discount doesn’t stack with B&N’s Premium Membership discount, and a few of the most popular new 4K releases are already out of stock online. We checked every price and stock status in this post on Barnes & Noble Wednesday afternoon, November 11.

A family movie night pick that holds up for the grown-ups

Plenty of family movies wear thin for the adults in the room by the fifth viewing, but The Princess Bride keeps getting quoted at dinner tables for a reason. The Criterion edition of The Princess Bride is $24.99 at Barnes & Noble, half of its $49.99 list price. B&N lists it as a 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray combo, so the standard disc covers any player in the house that can’t handle 4K. Rob Reiner’s 1987 fairy tale is a good place to start if you’re building a disc collection for a family that mostly streams.

The Coens’ Best Picture winner on 4K disc

Javier Bardem’s coin-flipping hitman is one of the scariest villains of the century, and the film around him won Best Picture. The No Country for Old Men 4K Blu-ray is $24.99, down from $49.99. Joel and Ethan Coen’s 2007 West Texas chase also stars Josh Brolin as the hunter who stumbles onto $2 million in drug money and Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff trying to keep up.

Akira Kurosawa made Yojimbo in 1961 and followed it with Sanjuro a year later, both starring Toshiro Mifune as the same scruffy, sharp-witted ronin. The Yojimbo/Sanjuro 4K Blu-ray set puts both films on 4K for $39.99, which works out to about $20 per movie. If Yojimbo’s plot sounds familiar, that’s because Sergio Leone borrowed it for A Fistful of Dollars. This set pairs well with the Seven Samurai 4K Blu-ray, which is $29.99.

Ten films, 20 discs and more than 25 hours of extras

This is the splurge pick in the sale, but per film it costs about the same as the single 4K discs and adds a Blu-ray copy of each movie. The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years is $249.99, half of its $499.99 list price, which comes to $25 per film. Criterion says the set includes ten 4K UHD discs in Dolby Vision HDR, ten Blu-rays and more than 25 hours of special features, running from Bottle Rocket through The French Dispatch. Every film in the set has new 4K masters supervised and approved by Anderson, according to Criterion.

The Princess Bride, No Country for Old Men and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs are $24.99, including Wall-E and David Lynch’s Mulholland Dr. A few older classics, like Citizen Kane, are $29.99. You need a 4K player to watch these discs, and our guide to the best Blu-ray players covers the 4K models worth buying.

The bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and they play on any Blu-ray player or game console with a disc drive. The KPop Demon Hunters Blu-ray is $19.99 and the KPop Demon Hunters DVD is $14.99, though its 4K edition is out of stock online. Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite is also $19.99.

The Wes Anderson Archive and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Box sets get the same 50 percent cut as single discs, and the big director collections are where the dollar savings add up. The 30-disc Ingmar Bergman’s Cinema set is $149.99, and the Essential Fellini set is $124.99.

#4628. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4627. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4626. Garmin and Waze just teamed up on a clever new way to keep cyclists safer

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

The new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Big Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

This is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one big limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

#4624. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.
